title: Your ReadyPlan
subtitle: 4 people · Long Island · 90 days · $1,500–5,000

sections.title: Household snapshot & planning assumptions
sections.summary: This plan covers 4 people in the Long Island area for a 90-day disruption. Every quantity below comes from the planning assumptions in this section.

blocks.caption: Local hazard profile (approximate, by ZIP prefix)

items: Water: 1 gal/adult/day, 0.75 gal/child/day, plus pets by size. Store up to 14 days; filter/collect beyond that.
Toilet paper: 1 roll/person/week. Diapers: 6/day per child in diapers.
Generator: 12 hours/day (furnace/boiler blower + ignition in cold weather, plus fridge and charging); inverter generator burns 0.25–0.4 gal gasoline/hour at ~half load.

sections.title: Priority list
sections.summary: Start with life safety this week, then water and food this month, then power and comfort. Check items off as you go.

blocks.text: This week

items.text: Test or install CO alarms: 4 (one per level plus outside sleeping areas).
Store your first 3 days of water: 12 gallons.
Turn on Wireless Emergency Alerts and sign up for your county's alert system.
Write the family communications plan (section 11) and pick an out-of-area contact.
Set aside $1,200 in small bills.
Find and label your main water shutoff, gas shutoff and electrical panel.
Buy 2 weeks of diapers (84) and wipes.
Keep every gas/diesel vehicle above half a tank from now on.

blocks.text: This month

items.text: Finish stored water: 54 gallons (8 7-gal jugs).

Buy Phase 1 gear: carbon monoxide alarm, 7-gallon water container, bathtub water bladder, unscented household bleach, hollow-fiber water filter, headlamps + led lanterns, aa/aaa battery stock, noaa weather radio, usb power bank, family first aid kit, fire extinguisher, fridge/freezer thermometers, indoor-rated portable propane heater, 1-lb propane cylinders (heater fuel), cold-rated sleeping bags, pipe insulation & faucet covers.
Build a 2-week pantry from the food list (about 98 thousand calories).
Get a licensed electrician's quote for a generator power inlet + interlock (or transfer switch) so the generator can safely run your furnace.
Do the pipe-freeze prep in section 5 (insulate exposed pipes, know how to drain lines).
Stock 2 weeks of pet food; ask your vet how to keep extra medication on hand if your pet takes any.
Pack a go-bag for each person (see the Evacuation section).
Check your flood zone and evacuation zone; review insurance (flood insurance has a 30-day wait).

blocks.text: Within 60 days

items.text: Complete the full 90 days food list: 653 lb of staples.
Buy the generator and fuel storage; test-run it outdoors, 20+ ft from the house, under load.
Set up water filtration + collection for days 15–90 (293 gallons).
Assemble the sanitation kit (two-bucket toilet, bags, absorbent).
Pre-cut and label window protection.

blocks.text: Within 90 days

items.text: Phase 3 items: comfort and communications upgrades.
Run a 'lights-out weekend': live off your plan for 24–48 hours and fix what breaks.
Drive the route to your raw land and back; note fuel stops and alternates.
Put the maintenance calendar on your phone.

sections.title: Day 0 checklist & decision triggers
sections.summary: When an outage or storm is coming, run this checklist. Once it hits, use the if/then table so decisions are made in advance, not under stress.

items.text: Check CO and smoke alarms; replace batteries if unsure.
Charge every phone, power bank and power station.
Fill the bathtub water bladder and spare containers.
Set fridge to its coldest setting; fill empty freezer space with water bottles.
Get cash and refill prescriptions if you can.
Fuel or charge vehicles.
Test-start the generator outdoors; stage fuel and cords.
Set up your warm room before the cold arrives (section 5).
Bring pets inside and stage their food, meds and carrier.
Check on elderly or disabled neighbors.

rows.if: A CO alarm sounds or anyone has headache, dizziness or nausea
rows.then: Everyone outside to fresh air now. Call 911. Don't go back in until responders say it's safe.

rows.if: Power is out more than 4 hours
rows.then: Discard refrigerated perishables that rose above 40°F. Keep the freezer closed (a full freezer holds about 48 hours).

rows.if: A boil-water notice is issued or tap water looks/smells wrong
rows.then: Use stored water; disinfect any other water (section 4).

rows.if: Indoor temperature drops below 55°F
rows.then: Move everyone into the warm room; close off the rest of the house.

rows.if: Indoor temperature drops below 45°F with no safe heat source
rows.then: Go to your fallback location or a warming center.

rows.if: Outdoor temperature forecast below 20°F during an outage
rows.then: Start the pipe-freeze protocol (section 5).

rows.if: Officials issue an evacuation order for your zone
rows.then: Leave. Take go-bags and pets to your fallback location.

rows.if: Sewage backs up or toilets can't flush
rows.then: Stop flushing; switch to the two-bucket toilet (section 9).

rows.if: A hurricane watch is issued
rows.then: Do the Day 0 checklist; put up window protection; decide stay vs. go before the warning.

sections.title: Your area's hazards
sections.summary: These are the hazards rated moderate or higher for the Long Island area, with the steps to take before and during each one.

blocks.text: Hurricane (high risk)

items.text: Look up your evacuation zone (county emergency site).
Photograph your home and belongings for insurance.
Know where to shut off power, gas and water.

rows.if: A hurricane watch is issued (about 48 hours out)
rows.then: Run the Day 0 checklist, fuel up, put up window protection, decide stay or go.

rows.if: You're told to evacuate, or you live in a mobile home or low-lying zone
rows.then: Leave early — before the warning. Roads jam fast.

rows.if: The eye passes and it goes calm
rows.then: Stay inside; the back half of the storm is coming.

blocks.text: Flooding (high risk)

items.text: Check whether you're in a flood zone at FEMA's Flood Map Service Center.
Flood damage usually isn't covered by homeowners insurance; flood policies have a 30-day wait.
Keep documents and valuables in waterproof bins up high.

rows.if: A flash flood warning is issued
rows.then: Move to higher ground now. Don't wait for water to rise.

rows.if: Water covers a road
rows.then: Turn around. Six inches of moving water can knock you down; a foot can float a car.

rows.if: Water is entering your home
rows.then: Turn off electricity at the main breaker only if you're dry and safe; otherwise leave it and get out.

sections.title: Water
sections.summary: Your household uses about 3.85 gallons a day. Store 54 gallons (14 days). After that, filter and disinfect collected water for the remaining 76 days.

rows.if: Tap water is still running and no advisory
rows.then: Use tap water first; save stored water.

rows.if: Boil-water notice
rows.then: Boil or disinfect tap water, or use stored water.

rows.if: No tap water
rows.then: Use stored water at 3.85 gal/day; use bathtub water for flushing.

rows.if: Stored water runs low
rows.then: Collect rain or surface water, filter it, then disinfect it.

blocks.title: How to disinfect water
blocks.text: EPA emergency disinfection: if water is cloudy, filter it first. Add 8 drops of regular unscented 6% bleach (or 6 drops of 8.25%) per gallon, stir, and wait 30 minutes. It should smell slightly of chlorine — if not, repeat once and wait another 15 minutes. Boiling for 1 full minute (3 minutes above 6,500 ft) also works.

items: Store water in food-grade containers away from sunlight and chemicals.
Replace tap-filled water every 6 months (mark the date).
Use a 0.1-micron filter for bacteria/protozoa, then disinfect for viruses.

sections.title: Heat & warmth
sections.summary: Winter is the most dangerous part of an outage in the Long Island area. Your plan uses a layered approach: keep the main heat running safely if you can, then shrink to one warm room, then relocate if it gets too cold.

blocks.text: Your natural gas heat needs electricity for the blower, ignition or circulator pump. The safest way to keep it running is a generator (recommended below) connected through a licensed electrician's power inlet and interlock (or a transfer switch). Furnaces draw roughly 400–800 W running, so a 2,500 W+ inverter generator can handle it along with the fridge.

blocks.title: Backup heater rules
blocks.text: Use only a propane heater labeled for indoor use with an oxygen depletion sensor (ODS) and tip-over shutoff, follow its manual's ventilation requirement, keep 3 feet of clearance, never leave it running while everyone sleeps, and keep a working CO alarm in the same room.

items: One warm room: pick a small interior room with few windows (not the basement if it floods). Everyone sleeps there.
Close doors to unused rooms; hang blankets over windows and doorways; put rugs/towels at door gaps.
Layer up: base layer, fleece, hat, socks; cold-rated sleeping bags at night.
Eat and drink warm calories; keep kids and older adults warm first.

blocks.caption: Pipe-freeze protocol
rows: Insulate exposed pipes; cover outdoor faucets; know where the main shutoff is.
Open cabinet doors under sinks; let faucets on outside walls drip.
Shut off the main water valve and open all faucets to drain lines (lowest first).
Shut off main water; call a plumber; move valuables; photograph damage for insurance.

rows.if: Furnace out and house above 55°F
rows.then: Close up the house, layer up, wait.

rows.if: House below 55°F
rows.then: Run the furnace from the generator via the inlet/interlock; or move to the warm room.

rows.if: Warm room still too cold
rows.then: Use the indoor-rated propane heater in that room with the CO alarm, following its manual.

rows.if: House below 45°F and dropping
rows.then: Relocate to a warming center, friends/family, or your fallback location.

blocks.title: Carbon monoxide
blocks.text: Never run a generator, grill, camp stove, charcoal or any fuel-burning device not rated for indoor use inside your home, garage, basement, crawlspace, tent or on a balcony — not even with doors or windows open. Keep generators outdoors at least 20 feet from doors, windows and vents, with the exhaust pointed away from buildings. Put battery-powered or battery-backup CO alarms on every level and outside sleeping areas. If a CO alarm sounds or anyone feels dizzy, headachy or nauseous, get everyone outside to fresh air right away and call 911.

sections.title: Power & fuel math
sections.summary: Plan on about 12 generator hours a day, burning 3–4.8 gallons of gasoline. Stored fuel of 30 gallons lasts about 6.3–10 days.

blocks.text: You don't have backup power yet. A dual-fuel inverter generator is the best value for your home; a battery power station covers quiet overnight loads.

blocks.caption: Fuel math at 12 hours/day (furnace/boiler blower + ignition in cold weather, plus fridge and charging)

items: Recommended stored gasoline for your scenario: 30 gal (6 5-gal cans) = 6.3–10 days of runtime.
Stretch fuel: run in blocks (for example 2 hours on, 2 off) — a full fridge stays cold for hours between runs.
Gasoline goes stale: add stabilizer and rotate into your cars every 12 months. Propane doesn't go stale, so it's better for long storage.
For a long outage you can't store enough gasoline: plan on propane cylinders, rationed runtime, and refueling when stations reopen.

rows.if: Power out, short outage expected
rows.then: Use power banks/power station; keep fridge closed.

rows.if: Power out more than 4 hours
rows.then: Set the generator outdoors 20+ ft from the house, exhaust away; run fridge/freezer cycles.

rows.if: Generator needs refueling
rows.then: Shut it off and let it cool for 15+ minutes before refueling.

rows.if: Rain or snow
rows.then: Use a generator tent/cover rated for it, still in open air — never move it into the garage.

rows.if: Utility lines down near home
rows.then: Stay 35+ ft away and call the utility.

blocks.title: Connecting a generator to your house
blocks.text: Never back-feed your house through a dryer outlet or any double-male ("suicide") cord — it can electrocute you, your neighbors and utility line workers, and start fires. Power house circuits only through a power inlet with an interlock or a transfer switch installed by a licensed electrician. Until then, plug appliances directly into the generator with outdoor-rated extension cords.

blocks.title: Carbon monoxide
blocks.text: Never run a generator, grill, camp stove, charcoal or any fuel-burning device not rated for indoor use inside your home, garage, basement, crawlspace, tent or on a balcony — not even with doors or windows open. Keep generators outdoors at least 20 feet from doors, windows and vents, with the exhaust pointed away from buildings. Put battery-powered or battery-backup CO alarms on every level and outside sleeping areas. If a CO alarm sounds or anyone feels dizzy, headachy or nauseous, get everyone outside to fresh air right away and call 911.

sections.title: Food
sections.summary: Your household needs about 7,000 calories a day — 630,000 for the full 90 days. The staples below provide it for roughly $1,234. Eat perishables first, then pantry food, then bulk staples.

blocks.caption: Eating order
rows: Normal meals; keep the fridge closed.
Fridge perishables that are still below 40°F, then freezer food (a full freezer holds ~48 h).
Pantry and canned food, ready-to-eat items.
Bulk staples: rice, beans, oats, pasta with oil, peanut butter, canned protein and produce.

items: Store staples in sealed food-grade buckets or mylar, cool and dry.
Include comfort foods, spices, and a manual can opener.

sections.title: Cooking & refrigeration
sections.summary: Plan how you'll cook without power and when to throw out fridge food. The four-hour rule keeps everyone from getting sick.

blocks.text: A gas range usually works in an outage if you light the burners with a match (check your manual; ovens with electronic controls usually won't work). Run the range hood or crack a window, and keep the CO alarm working.

rows.if: Fridge above 40°F for more than 4 hours
rows.then: Throw out meat, dairy, leftovers and cut produce. When in doubt, throw it out.

rows.if: Freezer food still has ice crystals or is at 40°F or below
rows.then: Safe to refreeze or cook.

rows.if: Running a generator
rows.then: Run fridge/freezer 1–2 hours at a time; keep doors shut between runs.

rows.if: Cooler use
rows.then: Keep it in the shade and packed with ice; check with a thermometer.

blocks.title: Cook outdoors only
blocks.text: Grills, camp stoves and charcoal give off carbon monoxide. Use them outdoors only — never inside, in a garage or on an enclosed porch.

sections.title: Sanitation, hygiene & diapers
sections.summary: Store 52 rolls of toilet paper and 540 diapers (6 a day). If toilets can't flush, switch to a two-bucket toilet.

blocks.text: Kids grow fast in a long scenario: half the diapers are in the next size up.

rows.if: Water and sewer working
rows.then: Flush normally; conserve water.

rows.if: No water but sewer OK
rows.then: Flush by pouring a bucket of non-drinking water into the bowl.

rows.if: Sewer backing up or officials say don't flush
rows.then: Line the toilet or a bucket with two bags, add absorbent after each use, tie off and store outside in a lidded can.

items: Wash hands with soap and water, or sanitizer when water is short.
Keep human waste away from food and water areas.

sections.title: First aid & medications
sections.summary: Keep a stocked first aid kit and a written list of everyone's medications and allergies. Talk to your doctor or pharmacist about keeping an extra supply.

items.text: Family first aid kit (bandages, gauze, tape, elastic wrap, gloves, shears, tweezers, thermometer).
Written list of each person's medications, doses as prescribed, allergies and doctors (keep with documents).
Over-the-counter basics you already use (pain/fever reducer, allergy, stomach) — check expiration dates.
Extra glasses/contacts, hearing aid batteries.
Children's versions of any OTC medicines you use, with the dosing tool that came in the box.
Take a Red Cross First Aid/CPR class.

blocks.title: Medications
blocks.text: ReadyPlan never gives medication doses. For any medicine — for people or pets — follow the label or your doctor, pharmacist or vet.

sections.title: Communications, cash & documents
sections.summary: Agree on how your family will reach each other, keep $1,200 in small bills, and keep copies of key documents in a waterproof pouch.

blocks.caption: Family communications plan (fill in)
rows: Raw land (~120 mi): address on paper in each go-bag
Who picks up, and the school's emergency plan

items: Text, don't call — texts get through congested networks.
NOAA weather radio for alerts when cell and internet are down.
FRS/GMRS radios for family and neighbors within a few miles (GMRS needs an FCC license, no exam).
Cash: $1,200 ($600 per adult) in small bills; card readers fail in outages.
Documents: copies of IDs, insurance policies, deeds/leases, medication list, pet records, and photos of your home's contents — in a waterproof pouch, plus an encrypted cloud copy.

sections.title: Security & neighbors
sections.summary: Keep a low profile and build a small neighbor pod. Neighbors who look out for each other are the best security in a long outage.

items: Low profile: don't post about your supplies; keep stored items out of sight; use curtains at night if you have lights when others don't.
Chain and lock the generator outdoors, in its safe spot 20+ ft from the house; it's loud and noticeable.
Lock doors and windows; keep exterior lights on a battery or solar motion light.
Neighbor pod: swap numbers with 3–5 nearby households, share skills (medical, tools, childcare), and check on older neighbors.
If you feel unsafe, leave and call 911. Supplies can be replaced; people can't.

sections.title: Kids & morale
sections.summary: Kids cope better when they have a routine and a job. Keep things predictable and give them a role in the plan.

items.text: Keep meal, nap and bedtime routines as close to normal as you can.
Give each child a 'job' (flashlight checker, water helper) so they feel useful.
Comfort kit: favorite stuffed animal/blanket, books, cards, coloring, glow sticks.
Put an ID card in each child's go-bag/pocket: name, parent phone numbers, out-of-area contact.
Practice the plan as a game: 'lights-out dinner', a family meeting-place walk.
Talk simply and honestly; limit news exposure; ask how they're feeling.
Toddlers: baby gates and covers near any heater or stove; extra outfits and sleep sacks for cold nights.

sections.title: Pets
sections.summary: Store 54 pounds of pet food and add 0.35 gallons of water a day for your pets. Keep records and a carrier ready.

items.text: Vaccination records and a recent photo of each pet (in the documents pouch).
Leash, harness, crate/carrier, collapsible bowls, waste bags or litter.
Microchip details up to date.
Know which shelters and hotels on your route accept pets.

blocks.title: Pet medications
blocks.text: ReadyPlan never gives medication doses. For any medicine — for people or pets — follow the label or your doctor, pharmacist or vet.

sections.title: Evacuation / bug-out plan
sections.summary: Your fallback is your raw land, about 120 miles away. Leave early on clear triggers, keep each tank above 7.2 gallons, and keep go-bags ready.

rows.if: Mandatory evacuation order for your zone
rows.then: Leave immediately.

rows.if: Hurricane warning and you're in an evacuation zone or a mobile/weak structure
rows.then: Leave before the warning window closes — roads fill fast.

rows.if: No heat, house below 45°F, and no restoration estimate
rows.then: Relocate while roads are passable.

rows.if: No water and no way to filter/collect
rows.then: Relocate.

rows.if: Home damaged or unsafe (gas smell, structural damage, flooding)
rows.then: Leave now; call 911/utility from a safe place.

rows.if: Roads closed or unsafe to drive
rows.then: Shelter in place and use this plan's shelter-in-place sections.

blocks.caption: Raw-land gear (nothing is there — bring it all)
rows: Family tent, 2 heavy tarps, paracord, stakes
Cold-rated sleeping bags, pads, wool blankets
Camp stove + propane (outdoor use only), pots, utensils
Bucket toilet kit, bags, shovel, toilet paper
Power station, solar panel, charging cables
Pantry + staples for the first week, cooler

blocks.text: Vehicle kit

items.text: Jump starter, tire inflator, tow strap
Paper road map with 2 routes marked
Blankets, water, snacks
Phone chargers
Flashlight, reflective triangles
Never store spare gasoline inside the car cabin

blocks.text: Go-bag (one per person)

items.text: Water (1 L) and filter bottle
3 days of snacks
Change of clothes, rain layer, hat, gloves
Headlamp + batteries
Medications (7-day supply), glasses
Copies of ID and medication list
Cash in small bills
Whistle, mask, hand sanitizer
Child ID card and comfort item
Pet food, leash, records

blocks.title: Tents and fumes
blocks.text: Never use a heater, stove, grill or generator inside a tent or vehicle. Cook and run generators in the open, away from where people sleep.

sections.title: Budget by phase
sections.summary: Within your $1,500–5,000 range we planned around $3,250. Phase 1 buys life safety first; the whole list comes to about $3,390.

rows: Phase 1 — life safety (CO alarms, water, heat)
Food staples, days 31–90 (build up with each grocery trip)

blocks.title: What to cut first
blocks.text: If money is tight, delay flood kit, pipe insulation & faucet covers, cold-rated sleeping bags. Never cut CO alarms, stored water, or your heat plan. Buy food a little at a time with each grocery trip.

sections.title: Maintenance calendar
sections.summary: Preparedness only works if it's maintained. Put these on your calendar now.

rows: Run the generator under load outdoors for 20 minutes.
Replace tap-filled stored water; check food dates and rotate into meals; refresh go-bags for the season.
Rotate stabilized gasoline into cars; replace bleach; check first aid kit; update documents, photos and medication lists.
Winter check: heat plan, pipe insulation, sleeping bags, propane.
Hurricane season check: window protection, evacuation zone, insurance, fuel.
Review this plan and regenerate it if your household changes.

disclaimer: ReadyPlan provides general preparedness guidance, not professional, medical, legal or electrical advice. Follow official instructions from local emergency management. Quantities are planning estimates. Prices and products change — check current specs, recalls and reviews before you buy.
